title: Klaus And Greta

jokes.text: did you dye your hair? / no.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jack if he dyed his hair, implying something looks different about him
jokes.punchline: Jack's flat 'no' — a one-word denial that closes the door on any follow-up, classic Jack stonewalling
jokes.explanation: Economical Jack character beat — his refusal to explain or elaborate is perfectly in character. Not exceptional but a solid cold-open tone-setter.

jokes.text: The wine turned out to be quite toxic.
jokes.setup: Jack describes his glamorous New Year's: 2,000-year-old Phoenician wine brought by famous deep-sea explorer Bob Ballard
jokes.punchline: Delivered with complete composure: 'The wine turned out to be quite toxic.'
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in Jack's comic voice: the escalating absurdity of the setup (ancient wine, famous explorer) makes the understated punchline land perfectly. The beat after — a pause before the reveal — is excellent structure. The deadpan delivery is character-specific: only Jack would treat poisoning his guests as a minor footnote. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: my guests and i spent the stroke of midnight in my garden. / vomiting.
jokes.setup: Jack continues the New Year's story, mentioning they spent midnight 'in my garden' — the patrician setting implies elegance
jokes.punchline: Beat. 'Vomiting.' — the word lands alone, after a pause, undercutting every aristocratic implication
jokes.explanation: The one-word sentence doing maximum structural work is exceptional economy. The rhythm — long elegant clause, pause, single gross word — is near-perfect sitcom construction. The joke earns its 8+ because the structure itself is doing the comedy, not just the content. It's the split-sentence beat that makes this excellent.

jokes.text: the whole night the purging, the new year, the vivid hallucinations of astarte the phoenician goddess of sex and war — it all wiped the slate clean.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining why he's at peace with his New Year's despite mass vomiting
jokes.punchline: He lists 'vivid hallucinations of Astarte the Phoenician goddess of sex and war' as a positive cleansing experience, delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Astarte the Phoenician goddess of sex and war' is where the laugh lives — the writers clearly researched the actual deity, and the 'sex and war' detail is funny in its own right. Only Jack would experience hallucinatory encounters with ancient deities and frame it as spiritually restorative. High character integration.

jokes.text: my cousin randy, this kid from this rural coal mining town, came out to us. And I think old liz lemon had a little something to do with that.
jokes.setup: Liz recounts her family New Year's as 'very special' — her cousin came out to the family
jokes.punchline: She self-aggrandizingly takes credit for a gay man's coming out
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon self-deception played perfectly — she genuinely believes she was an inspiration for her cousin's sexuality. Good character integration; slightly undercut by being a familiar Liz beat.

jokes.text: randy's gay, everybody! / he's gay. / i think everyone knew. / finally!
jokes.setup: Liz excitedly announces her cousin's coming out to the TGS staff
jokes.punchline: The staff's complete indifference — 'I think everyone knew' and 'Finally!' — deflates her excitement perfectly
jokes.explanation: The rapid deflation of Liz's excitement via the ensemble is well-timed. 'Finally!' is the better of the two reactions — implies the room saw this coming for years. Efficient multi-person beat.

jokes.text: over the break, i forgot what floor i worked on. / six, tracy. / six! I knew it was a character from Blossom, but i couldn't find the joey russo button.
jokes.setup: Tracy casually mentions he forgot what floor he works on
jokes.punchline: He tried to find the floor by looking for a 'Joey Russo button' — Joey Russo being a character from the 90s show Blossom, played by Joey Lawrence (floor six = '6' but Tracy's brain accessed '6' via Blossom cast)
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great joke. Tracy's brain associating the number 6 with Joey Russo from Blossom — and specifically looking for an elevator button — is absurdist gold that ONLY Tracy Jordan could deliver. The specificity of 'Joey Russo button' is hilarious and odd enough to stick. Perfectly integrates his character as someone who processes reality through a filter of random celebrity pop culture. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: i met james franco's manager. / it was like a fairy tale.
jokes.setup: Jenna dramatically announces her amazing New Year's
jokes.punchline: The amazing thing was meeting a manager, not the star — and she calls it a fairy tale
jokes.explanation: Good Jenna beat — her version of 'amazing' is meeting an agent adjacent to a star. The fairy tale framing is a nice ironic touch. Sets up the premise economically.

jokes.text: are you available for a fake romance with a movie star? / does chewing on a sponge trick your brain's hunger center? / yes! yes! a million times yes!
jokes.setup: The manager asks Jenna if she's available for a fake Hollywood romance
jokes.punchline: Jenna answers by asking if chewing on a sponge tricks your hunger center — implying she does this — and then screams yes
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The sponge line is a perfect non-sequitur that reveals Jenna's eating-disordered, fame-hungry desperation in a single absurd image. That she uses this as an analogy — 'yes, obviously' — is deeply Jenna. Then the triple 'yes! yes! a million times yes!' seals it with performative excess. Highly quotable. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: can you believe they went to me before ayiiia from the real world: cancun?
jokes.setup: Jenna is marveling that she was selected for the fake romance
jokes.punchline: Her reference point for 'a lower choice than me' is a random Real World cast member from a specific season — implying her self-assessment of fame is calibrated to reality TV minor celebrities
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Ayiiia from The Real World: Cancun' is precise and funny — it's a real cast member, which makes the joke land harder. Jenna's self-image as barely above reality TV micro-celebrities is perfectly character-consistent and gently devastating.

jokes.text: lemon, i want you and jenna to have a meeting with james franco and make sure his manager doesn't screw her. / too late! / wait, which way did you mean that?
jokes.setup: Jack says he wants Liz to make sure the manager doesn't 'screw' Jenna
jokes.punchline: Jenna's 'Too late!' followed by Liz's 'Which way did you mean that?' — the double entendre plays both ways
jokes.explanation: A functional double entendre — Jenna's 'too late' is a good read on the joke but the structure is well-worn. Liz adding the clarification extends it adequately. Not inspired but earns a solid laugh.

jokes.text: my wife and i are trying for a daughter, and on new year's eve i think i got angie pregnant. / no, no, no, no. / okay, but i was gonna describe it real good.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces he may have gotten Angie pregnant on New Year's Eve and implies he's going to share details
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately shuts him down; Tracy's protest is that he was going to 'describe it real good' — as if the quality of the description is the issue
jokes.explanation: 'I was gonna describe it real good' is a deceptively perfect Tracy line. The specificity of 'real good' implies Tracy's idea of sharing news is essentially a vivid verbal performance, and his disappointment at being stopped is completely earnest. Totally character-specific.

jokes.text: how was your new year's, sir? / perfect. / oh my god!
jokes.setup: Jonathan asks Jack how his New Year's was as a standard pleasantry
jokes.punchline: Jack says 'perfect' — to which Jonathan reacts with 'oh my god!' of genuine awe, as if Jack's holiday being perfect is a revelation worthy of worship
jokes.explanation: Quick efficient joke on Jonathan's sycophantic devotion to Jack. 'Oh my god' as a response to 'perfect' is Jonathan's character in one beat. Good economy.

jokes.text: as you know, on new year's, i finally met my birth parents. / so. / thank you for asking about that!
jokes.setup: Kenneth mentions he finally met his birth parents — a huge life event — and waits for follow-up
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'So.' followed by a pivot to his own problems, and Kenneth's passive-aggressive 'thank you for asking about that!' — all delivered without any malice from either party
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed three-beat joke. Kenneth's 'as you know' setup signals he's been waiting to share this, Jack's 'So.' is cartoonishly dismissive without being mean (he genuinely just has other priorities), and Kenneth's 'thank you for asking about that!' lands as passive-aggressive politeness — a Kenneth-specific reaction. All three beats are character-perfect. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: damn that phoenician wine!
jokes.setup: Jack reveals he drunkenly called Nancy at 3:42 AM and can't remember it
jokes.punchline: 'Damn that Phoenician wine!' — blaming the 2,000-year-old toxic wine for his drunk dial
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback economy. Five words recalling an entire elaborate setup. The comedy is in the grandiosity — blaming ancient Phoenician wine for a drunk dial is absurdly specific and very Jack. The callback rewards attentive viewers.

jokes.text: the last thing i remember is going into a closet and switching clothes with bob ballard.
jokes.setup: Jack explains his blackout from the toxic wine
jokes.punchline: His last memory is exchanging clothes with famous oceanographer Bob Ballard in a closet — a surreal detail offered deadpan
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Bob Ballard makes this gold — not just 'a friend' but the real-world Titanic explorer. Why are they swapping clothes? The joke doesn't explain and doesn't need to. The image is funny precisely because it's unexplained.

jokes.text: the woman is on vacation with her husband as we speak, probably having beach sex, which is the third best sex after elevator and white house.
jokes.setup: Jack is agonizing over Nancy being in Florida with her husband
jokes.punchline: He has a ranked taxonomy of sex locations — beach is third, behind elevator and white house — delivered as established fact
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Jack has a personal, confident ranking of best sex locations, and 'white house' as the #2 slot is the detail that makes it exceptional — it implies Jack has had sex in the White House, which he states casually as context. The rankings format is absurd but delivered with Jack's characteristic authority. Extremely quotable and character-defining. High marks across all craft dimensions.

jokes.text: as a frequent leaver of drunken messages, i can tell you no good can come of this. / as a frequent receiver of drunk messages, they are not cute, even when they're from liz.
jokes.setup: They're discussing whether Nancy has heard Jack's drunk voicemail
jokes.punchline: Liz's self-identification as a 'frequent leaver' of drunk messages, then Cerie's immediate counter-admission as a 'frequent receiver' — specifically noting Liz's messages aren't cute
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat joke with the Liz-Cerie dynamic — Cerie's casual cruelty ('even when they're from Liz') is perfectly in her character as someone who treats Liz as a social cautionary tale without even meaning to be mean. Well-constructed parallel structure.

jokes.text: good lord, i've lemoned the situation with nancy! / 'lemoned'? that's not a thing people are saying now, is it? / cerie? / lemoned. doing it awesome.
jokes.setup: Jack coins a new verb — 'lemoned' — to describe having made a mess of a situation, then worries it's slang he's missed
jokes.punchline: He asks Cerie to verify; Cerie lies ('doing it awesome') to please him, implying the word isn't real but Jack now believes it is
jokes.explanation: Wonderful meta-joke. 'Lemoned' as a verb meaning 'to royally screw something up' is both character-defining for Liz and reveals Jack's status anxiety about slang. Cerie enabling the delusion with 'doing it awesome' is a perfect third beat. The joke also works as meta-commentary on the show itself naming its own disaster formula after its protagonist. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: you and i pretend we met while filming a movie called Space Attack. / my title.
jokes.setup: James Franco is laying out the fake romance cover story involving a fictional film
jokes.punchline: 'My title.' — Franco's pride in the terrible movie title, delivered as a casual aside
jokes.explanation: Quick two-word joke with great economy. The terrible, generic title and Franco's proprietary pride in it is a funny character detail — satirizing the kind of high-concept lowbrow blockbuster titles that actually exist.

jokes.text: this movie will never be released because my performance will be deemed 'too provocative for america.' / oh, i wish i lived in france.
jokes.setup: Franco explains the fake movie will never be released
jokes.punchline: His reason is that he's 'too provocative for America'; Jenna's response is sincere longing for France as the land of acceptable provocativeness
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke playing on celebrity self-regard (Franco's grandiosity) and Jenna's performative artiste identity (wanting to live in France). Both land cleanly. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: five dates a week, one fight a month. and because of a product placement deal with jamba juice, the fight will be in a jamba juice.
jokes.setup: The manager is outlining the terms of the fake romance
jokes.punchline: The contractual fight is sponsored by Jamba Juice, including location
jokes.explanation: Sharp Hollywood satire. The idea that a fake-celebrity-couple fight would be sponsored and location-contracted is both absurd and disturbingly plausible. The Jamba Juice specificity is funny in itself — it's a real brand that feels oddly pedestrian for a glamorous romance.

jokes.text: i love jamba juice!
jokes.setup: The manager mentions the contractual Jamba Juice fight
jokes.punchline: Jenna's delighted, non-sequitur enthusiasm for Jamba Juice as if this is the best part of the deal
jokes.explanation: Short efficient laugh — Jenna's enthusiasm for the smoothie brand amid contract negotiations is a small but real character beat showing her priorities.

jokes.text: are you familiar with japanese moe relationships, where socially dysfunctional men develop deep emotional attachments to body pillows with women painted on them? / i am not, james. / neither am i, liz! which is why it's so weird the tabloids are running all these stories saying i'm in love with a body pillow.
jokes.setup: Liz asks what Franco is covering up; he launches into a detailed, specific explanation of body pillow romance subculture while disavowing it
jokes.punchline: 'Neither am I, Liz!' — his instant mirroring denial after Liz says she's unfamiliar, combined with the fact that he explained it in forensic detail
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of the better celebrity-guest jokes in 30 Rock's run. Franco explaining the moe phenomenon with expert-level specificity, then immediately claiming ignorance when Liz says she doesn't know it, is perfectly constructed dramatic irony. The joke works on multiple levels: the absurdity of the premise, Franco's transparent denial, and the deadpan pace. 'Neither am I, Liz!' is the peak — the exact mirroring of her line is the structural key. Genuinely exceptional.

jokes.text: then why is that here? / why? i mean, why is this table here? i mean, why is that lamp here? kimiko is — it is here like any other object.
jokes.setup: Presumably the body pillow (Kimiko) is visible in the room; Liz asks why it's there
jokes.punchline: Franco's desperate false equivalence — comparing the pillow to a table and a lamp, then almost using her name before self-correcting to 'it'
jokes.explanation: The self-correction from 'Kimiko' to 'it' is the surgical precision of the joke — Franco's denial slipping to reveal the name and then the scramble to recover. The escalating false equivalences (table, lamp) are well-paced absurdist deflection. Strong construction.

jokes.text: objects are made by men and used for many purposes. / but we never love objects. / where do i sign?
jokes.setup: Franco continues his speech about not loving objects (the pillow)
jokes.punchline: Jenna, completely charmed by this strange man's obvious lie, immediately asks to sign the contract
jokes.explanation: Jenna's 'where do I sign?' after Franco's most suspicious speech is a good character beat — she's utterly uncritical when fame is involved. Clean button to the scene.

jokes.text: there's a guy here who offered to drive me if i helped him move a couch into a van. / nope. that's a serial killer.
jokes.setup: Randy mentions a ride offer involving moving a couch into a van
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate, flat: 'Nope. That's a serial killer.' — a classically recognized serial killer scenario stated as obvious fact
jokes.explanation: Efficient joke on the well-known serial killer trope; Liz's flatly stated expertise is funny. The joke isn't original (the van-with-couch scenario is familiar) but the deadpan delivery and perfect economy earn it.

jokes.text: you have amish here?
jokes.setup: Liz tells Randy to get in a cab
jokes.punchline: Randy sees something on the street and asks if there are Amish people in New York, revealing his small-town naivete — probably seeing a Hasidic Jewish person
jokes.explanation: Quick visual/character gag. Randy's rural Pennsylvania confusion is efficient and the implicit subject (likely Hasidic men) adds a layer without spelling it out. Good economy.

jokes.text: kenneth, jonathan, i need one of you to help me with a very special assignment. / i hope it's me. / but i'm honored just to be standing here with you.
jokes.setup: Jack asks for a volunteer for a special assignment
jokes.punchline: Both Kenneth and Jonathan express extreme eagerness; Jonathan's 'honored just to be standing here with you' is especially sycophantic
jokes.explanation: Good double-character beat on the Jonathan/Kenneth worship of Jack. Jonathan's line is funnier — 'honored just to be standing here' implies he has no expectation of usefulness, just physical proximity to Jack as its own reward.

jokes.text: i'm going to drive up to waltham, massachusetts, break into a woman's home, and erase a potentially embarrassing and destructive answering machine message. the home in question has a doggy door. that will be our way in.
jokes.setup: Jack is framing a home-break-in mission
jokes.punchline: Jack lays out a criminal plan with the gravitas and logistics of a corporate strategy presentation, treating the doggy door as a tactical asset
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Jack — treating a criminal enterprise with businesslike precision. 'That will be our way in' as the climax of a briefing on a doggy door is absurdly good. The juxtaposition of Jack's authority register with the absurd mission is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: using these hangers, prove that you are lithe enough to accompany me to waltham. [Kenneth successfully squeezes through] / it's kenneth! / [Jonathan fails] / you sicken me.
jokes.setup: Jack holds up coat hangers and challenges Kenneth and Jonathan to demonstrate they can fit through a doggy door
jokes.punchline: Kenneth succeeds (visual); Jonathan fails and gets 'you sicken me' — Jack's disgust at Jonathan's physical inadequacy
jokes.explanation: Strong visual comedy sequence. The audition-via-hanger is absurd, Kenneth winning is a perfect inversion (the lanky country kid wins), and 'you sicken me' is Jack at his most imperious. The physical comedy plus Jack's disgust makes this a high-energy sequence.

jokes.text: i just had a burrito!
jokes.setup: Tracy announces Angie is pregnant and then says 'it gets better'
jokes.punchline: The thing that 'gets better' is that he just had a burrito — placed on the same level as impending fatherhood
jokes.explanation: A pure Tracy joke — the burrito achieving equal importance to a pregnancy announcement is exactly how his mind works. 'It gets better' as a setup for 'I just had a burrito' is structurally perfect misdirection. The escalation of the setup against the mundanity of the punchline is sublime Tracy characterization. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: i know it's a girl, liz lemon, because i yelled 'susan b. anthony' at the moment of conception.
jokes.setup: Tracy says he knows the baby will be a girl
jokes.punchline: His method of sex determination: yelling Susan B. Anthony's name at conception — delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The specificity of Susan B. Anthony is inexplicably perfect — not just any feminist icon, but that specific historical figure, yelled at the moment of conception as a folk sex-determination method. Only Tracy Jordan has this brand of confident absurdist logic, and his delivery of 'I know it's a girl, Liz Lemon, because' makes you expect some street-logic rationale, not THIS. The joke is maximally character-specific, maximally original, and perfectly economical. This is what a 9+ looks like.

jokes.text: we're gonna name her after the place she was conceived. it was a pretty wild night. so we gonna name her either virginia, netjet, or bathroom at teterboro airport.
jokes.setup: Tracy says they'll name the daughter after where she was conceived
jokes.punchline: The three options escalate in specificity and absurdity: Virginia (normal), NetJet (corporate aviation), Bathroom at Teterboro Airport (a specific New Jersey private airport bathroom)
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect escalation joke. Starting with 'Virginia' lulls the audience before the list pivots to a private jet service and a specific airport bathroom. The escalation structure is textbook — each option is funnier and more specific than the last. 'Bathroom at Teterboro Airport' as a candidate baby name is specific enough to hurt. Excellent.

jokes.text: virginia is nice.
jokes.setup: Tracy lists three increasingly absurd baby name options
jokes.punchline: Liz's small, polite approval of only 'Virginia' — completely ignoring the other two options as if they were live candidates
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Tracy bit. Three words that accept the bizarre framing of the joke, treating 'Virginia is nice' as a totally reasonable name shortlist opinion. Liz's normalization of Tracy's insanity is a consistent comic rhythm.

jokes.text: you and i are not getting any younger. / you don't know that thing i sleep in isn't working.
jokes.setup: Liz tries to prompt Jenna toward real romance, noting they're aging
jokes.punchline: Jenna counters by suggesting her 'thing she sleeps in' (presumably a beauty/age-reversing device) might be working
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Jenna-specific deflection. The deliberately vague 'thing I sleep in' implies something bizarre (hyperbaric chamber? Oxygen tent? Cocoon?) that she refuses to name, suggesting extreme vanity tech. The joke is funnier for what it doesn't say. Jenna's denial of aging is perfectly consistent with her character.

jokes.text: all this attention, getting my picture taken, having ice cold diarrhea from drinking too much jamba juice — it's everything i ever wanted.
jokes.setup: Jenna says she's happy with the fake relationship
jokes.punchline: Her list of happiness sources includes 'ice cold diarrhea from too much Jamba Juice' as a natural item alongside fame perks
jokes.explanation: A callback that pays off beautifully. The Jamba Juice joke is now weaponized — the sponsored fighting location has resulted in overconsumption and specific, graphic GI distress, which Jenna lists as happiness. Her complete acceptance of this as a positive is exactly who she is. 'Ice cold diarrhea' as a specific modifier is a great gross-out detail that earns its place.

jokes.text: sorry, sir. that happens sometimes when i unhinge my pelvis.
jokes.setup: Implied physical comedy — Kenneth has presumably done something strange, possibly contorting to fit through something as practice for the break-in
jokes.punchline: 'That happens sometimes when I unhinge my pelvis.' — the casual normalizing of a physically impossible/disturbing anatomical feature
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great Kenneth joke. 'Unhinge my pelvis' casually stated as a natural occurrence that sometimes happens taps into the show's long-running mythology about Kenneth not being fully human. The deadpan apology to Jack adds a layer. Highly quotable and a great deepening of Kenneth's unsettling physical comedy.

jokes.text: it's not an answering machine, it's a voice mail. / okay, well, we just need to look for clues to her password. it'll be like the da vinci code. / ehh, albino monk!
jokes.setup: They've broken into Nancy's house and face a voicemail password
jokes.punchline: Jack says it'll be like The Da Vinci Code; Kenneth immediately yells 'albino monk!' — apparently his main takeaway from the book/film is the albino villain
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's 'albino monk!' as a Da Vinci Code password attempt is both funny as a non-sequitur guess and character-consistent — Kenneth's unsophisticated pop culture processing produces 'albino monk' as the essential fact of the entire thriller. The enthusiasm of the exclamation sells it.

jokes.text: i just took my picture with that little camera thing. / kenneth! / all right. i just need to erase that picture. / whoops, i just made it the desktop image. how did i do that?
jokes.setup: Kenneth is trying to use Nancy's computer to find the password
jokes.punchline: Kenneth accidentally takes a selfie, then accidentally makes it the desktop wallpaper — escalating technological incompetence
jokes.explanation: Good escalation on Kenneth's techno-incompetence — it gets worse with each step. 'How did I do that?' is genuinely funny as baffled self-inquiry. Not groundbreaking but a solid laugh-getter.

jokes.text: 'emailing image to address book'? / what is wrong with me?
jokes.setup: Kenneth has already taken a selfie and made it the desktop; now he's emailing it to everyone in the address book
jokes.punchline: 'What is wrong with me?' — Kenneth's genuine self-interrogation as the disaster continues to compound
jokes.explanation: The third beat of the computer escalation. 'What is wrong with me?' captures Kenneth's genuine bafflement at his own actions — he's not being malicious, just catastrophically inadept. Good escalation payoff.

jokes.text: nancy's husband has been sleeping on the couch.
jokes.setup: While snooping through Nancy's house, Jack discovers the sleeping arrangements
jokes.punchline: The simple discovery is delivered as the most significant intelligence of the mission — the couch reveals a marriage in trouble
jokes.explanation: More plot-driven than comedically inventive, but the visual beat of Jack deducing a failing marriage from a throw pillow on a couch during a break-in has a dark comedy quality.

jokes.text: that's where i'm meeting them later — a bar called 'home butt.'
jokes.setup: Liz says she's glad Randy's new friends brought him home
jokes.punchline: Randy reveals the bar is named 'Home Butt' — a clearly gay bar name that Randy either doesn't parse or doesn't care about
jokes.explanation: The bar name is a satisfying joke — 'Home Butt' is not subtle, and Randy's complete obliviousness (or acceptance) to it reveals his newness to gay culture. The innocence of his delivery is the comedy.

jokes.text: the local tv station edited will & grace down so much that it was just called 'karen.'
jokes.setup: Randy explains how hard it was growing up gay in rural Pennsylvania
jokes.punchline: The local TV censored Will & Grace so heavily — removing the gay content — that only the heterosexual supporting character Karen remained
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes — possibly in the top tier of the entire series. The premise (a conservative TV station editing Will & Grace until only Karen remained) is both a precise social satire of rural censorship and an excellent meta-joke about television. Karen is the most flamboyant, least-family-friendly character on the show — the joke reveals the absurdity of the editing agenda. The economy is extraordinary: one sentence does enormous cultural work. Highly quotable and genuinely clever.

jokes.text: we're gonna stay here and make nachos and see who can fall asleep the earliest.
jokes.setup: Randy wants to go out and enjoy New York; Liz offers an alternative
jokes.punchline: Liz's idea of fun is competitive early sleeping and nachos — presented as a genuine fun offer
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon self-portrait. 'See who can fall asleep the earliest' as a competitive activity is one of the show's core Liz jokes — her idea of fun is essentially low-grade inertia. The specificity of it being a competition makes it land harder.

jokes.text: your hand feels like a pillow that's been in the microwave.
jokes.setup: Jenna is holding Randy's hand — perhaps during the nachos / sleepover hangout
jokes.punchline: Randy's oddly specific compliment: 'a pillow that's been in the microwave' — warm, soft, weird
jokes.explanation: The simile is strange in the best way — microwaved pillow is an oddly cozy and specific image that lands as genuine small-town sincerity. The joke is in the precision of the weirdness.

jokes.text: that was fake. / did you know 'paparazzo' is singular to 'paparazzi'? / kimiko taught me that.
jokes.setup: After a fake PDA moment, Franco breaks the fourth wall of their arrangement, then offers a word origin fact
jokes.punchline: 'Kimiko taught me that.' — the body pillow is now credited as an Italian linguistics teacher
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Franco's casual attribution of a language lesson to his body pillow deepens the joke — Kimiko is now not just a love interest but an educational resource. The confidence and non-defensiveness of 'Kimiko taught me that' implies a rich domestic life. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: if you type 'nancy's secrets' into the internet, do you have any idea what comes up? / a store that sells wig extensions.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is trying to find Nancy's password online and makes an attempt
jokes.punchline: Typing 'Nancy's Secrets' into a search engine yields a wig extension store — completely useless, but also exactly what you'd get
jokes.explanation: Decent laugh from the mundane search result — a wig extension store is a specific, realistic outcome of a vague search term. Jack's exasperation is the delivery vehicle.

jokes.text: i've seen all this before, kenneth. the separate beds, the empty closets, the brave public face. this is just another irish catholic couple who won't admit to the world that their marriage is over.
jokes.setup: Kenneth protests that they don't know Nancy's marriage is bad
jokes.punchline: Jack delivers a sociological taxonomy of Irish Catholic marital denial, as if it's a distinct cultural phenomenon he's catalogued
jokes.explanation: Good Jack character moment — his Bostonian Catholic background gives him specific cultural authority to diagnose a failed Irish marriage. 'Brave public face' as a stage in this taxonomy is precise and funny.

jokes.text: nancy donovan, still so organized. in german class, mr. kruger always chose her to sort the students. / he was eventually arrested by israeli commandos.
jokes.setup: Jack wistfully remembers Nancy from high school — she was organized enough to sort students
jokes.punchline: 'He was eventually arrested by Israeli commandos.' — implying the German teacher who had students sort each other by category was a Nazi war criminal; the punchline is barely a sentence
jokes.explanation: The episode's crown jewel. The setup is innocuous — a nostalgic memory about an organized classmate — until 'he was eventually arrested by Israeli commandos.' The joke earns its dark subversion through perfect structural patience: the setup never hints at where it's going. The Israeli commandos line is historically specific (referencing the Mossad's Nazi-hunting operations), which grounds the dark joke in real history while being maximally economical. The whole Holocaust is implied in six words without a single explicit reference. This is what a 9+ looks like — it's genuinely among the more daring, well-constructed jokes in the show's run.

jokes.text: uh, fort myers and cincinnati. did you not learn your nation's airport codes in high school?
jokes.setup: Kenneth can't identify airport codes RSW and CVG
jokes.punchline: Jack is incredulous that Kenneth doesn't know airport codes as if this is basic civic education
jokes.explanation: Jack's assumption that airport codes are standard high school curriculum is a great class/privilege joke. The implication is that Jack's elite upbringing included this as routine knowledge. Good character-specific arrogance.

jokes.text: she's at the beach house alone! / that's the most divorced sentence i've ever heard.
jokes.setup: Jack deduces from separate flight records that Nancy is vacationing alone
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's 'That's the most divorced sentence I've ever heard' — a beautifully economical observation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. 'That's the most divorced sentence I've ever heard' is a perfect Kenneth reaction — unexpectedly perceptive coming from the show's most innocent character. The superlative construction ('the most divorced sentence') is a great comic formula. Maximum economy, maximum quotability. Earns high marks.

jokes.text: oh my god, did you go out last night after i won the sleeping contest?
jokes.setup: Liz notices Randy came home late and had adventures
jokes.punchline: She refers to falling asleep first as 'winning the sleeping contest' — treating the nachos-and-sleep night as a genuine competition she prevailed in
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback and Liz characterization — she genuinely competed at falling asleep and won, and is proud of it. The callback reward is immediate: we laugh harder because we remember the setup. 'I won the sleeping contest' is a great quotable.

jokes.text: i forgot to wash my face, didn't i? / i meant to do it at the club, / but when i got into the bathroom, everything started up again.
jokes.setup: Randy comes home clearly having been out all night, and Liz notes he didn't wash his face
jokes.punchline: His excuse is that he meant to wash his face at the club bathroom, but 'everything started up again' — an innuendo about what happens in a gay club bathroom
jokes.explanation: A mild innuendo joke about Randy's exploits told through the polite framing of face-washing logistics. The indirection is the joke — 'everything started up again' covers a lot of ground without specifying. Functional.

jokes.text: okay, that's it, i am taking you to the port authority. / to get on a bus home, not to meet people!
jokes.setup: Liz decides Randy needs to go home
jokes.punchline: She preemptively clarifies what the Port Authority is for — knowing Randy would find romantic prospects there — adding 'not to meet people'
jokes.explanation: Good joke on the Port Authority's reputation as a cruising location — Liz's anticipatory clarification reveals how quickly she's adapted to Randy's worldview. The defensive addition 'not to meet people!' is the punch.

jokes.text: is it gonna be fierce? / it would be if it was 2006.
jokes.setup: Randy enthusiastically asks if the makeover will be 'fierce' — using gay slang
jokes.punchline: Liz deflates the slang by dating it: 'it would be if it was 2006' — 'fierce' peaked with Project Runway/America's Next Top Model circa 2006
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural observation about the shelf life of gay slang — 'fierce' had a very specific 2005-2007 peak. Liz's encyclopedic knowledge of pop culture expiration dates is perfect for her character. Efficient and funny.

jokes.text: i'm not going back to methenburg! / randy lemon, you open this door right now! / okay, i do appreciate the irony that i'm the one stuck in the closet now. / is that irony? / not really.
jokes.setup: Randy locks himself in a room to avoid going home; Liz notes the irony of being 'stuck in the closet'
jokes.punchline: Liz raises the 'irony' of a gay man's cousin being stuck in a closet, then immediately self-questions 'is that irony?' and Liz concedes 'not really' — the joke mocks its own wordplay
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke that eats itself — Liz makes the closet/gay pun, immediately questions whether it qualifies as irony, and Liz admits it doesn't. The self-awareness about the quality of the joke is funnier than the joke itself would have been. 30 Rock loves puncturing its own setups. Very well-constructed.

jokes.text: the sun is up and we are still in these people's home. / god can see us now.
jokes.setup: They've spent the night breaking into Nancy's house
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's moral concern activates specifically at sunrise — God can now see them — implying darkness provided cover from divine observation
jokes.explanation: A wonderful Kenneth-specific theological joke. His logic is absurd but internally consistent: darkness = divine blindspot. The specificity of 'God can see us now' as the activating moral concern — not 'the neighbors can see us' or 'this is illegal' — is deeply Kenneth. Highly quotable and character-defining.

jokes.text: we have to find that voice mail code. / it's on the dry erase board above the phone. / what? / i saw it there a few hours ago. / but i wasn't done looking around.
jokes.setup: Jack has been searching the entire house for the voicemail code
jokes.punchline: Kenneth saw it immediately but said nothing because Jack 'wasn't done looking around' — Kenneth was too deferential to stop the boss's enjoyment of snooping
jokes.explanation: A great beat on both Kenneth's deference and Jack's nosiness. Kenneth spotted the code right away but correctly intuited that Jack was enjoying himself snooping, so he let it continue. The revelation recontextualizes the entire house search as pointless Jack voyeurism that Kenneth accommodated. Excellent character work for both.

jokes.text: sir, i don't mean to swear, but i am irritated right now.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is frustrated with the break-in situation
jokes.punchline: 'I don't mean to swear, but I am irritated right now' — Kenneth prefacing mild irritation with a swearing warning, when no actual swearing follows
jokes.explanation: A perfect Kenneth line. The construction is ideal: 'I don't mean to swear' raises the expectation of profanity, then 'but I am irritated right now' delivers what is, for Kenneth, essentially the equivalent. It's Kenneth's maximum anger expressed through his permanent filter of politeness. The joke is entirely in the gap between the warning and the delivery. Character-specific to the molecular level.

jokes.text: you were gretta and i was klaus / jack, are you coming in? / i'm on the phone! / get back in the hot tub. / ballard, don't let them put their tops back on.
jokes.setup: We're hearing Jack's drunk New Year's voicemail — a tender, romantic message to Nancy
jokes.punchline: Halfway through a romantic speech, Jack breaks to shout at people at the hot tub party ('Ballard, don't let them put their tops back on'), then resumes the message
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction: the romantic voicemail is interrupted by party-hosting, specifically Bob Ballard (callback!) managing the hot tub. 'Ballard, don't let them put their tops back on' is Jack ordering his oceanographer friend to enforce toplessness while leaving a sincere love message. The tonal juxtaposition is perfectly Jack and the Ballard callback rewards attentive viewing.

jokes.text: but you are leaving through the doggy door.
jokes.setup: Jack agrees with Kenneth's wisdom and thanks him
jokes.punchline: Despite the touching moment, Jack insists Kenneth exits through the doggy door — maintaining hierarchy even in gratitude
jokes.explanation: A button with real sting — Jack's warmth toward Kenneth is instantly undercut by insisting on the doggy door exit. It's both a callback and a character joke: Jack's respect for Kenneth has absolute limits determined by station. 'Yes, sir.' as Kenneth's response makes it land even harder.

jokes.text: hey, liz, we're playing the today show drinking game. you do a shot every time they give a dumb travel tip. / i like to take the shampoo and put it in the little travel size bottles. / then i take the original bottle and put it back in the shower. / for later.
jokes.setup: Tracy is playing a Today Show drinking game based on dumb travel tips
jokes.punchline: The 'tip' shown: taking shampoo from the big bottle into travel sizes, then putting the original back 'for later' — the tip saves nothing and describes normal behavior as a money-saving hack
jokes.explanation: Sharp media satire. The Today Show's travel tip is completely useless — the 'advice' is to put shampoo in a bottle and then put the original back, which accomplishes nothing. 'For later' as the punchline button is perfect, implying the tip-giver thinks keeping the original shampoo is the insight. Good TV industry mockery.

jokes.text: we're in love! / trent's quitting the navy, and we're going to get married in massachusetts. / congratulations. / oh boy. / if you want to save money on the trip, consider taking a sandwich.
jokes.setup: A gay couple announces on the Today Show they're getting married in Massachusetts
jokes.punchline: The anchor's response to a milestone civil rights moment is 'if you want to save money on the trip, consider taking a sandwich' — the travel tip format trivializes the moment
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and media satire. The Today Show format continues into a gay marriage announcement — the anchor's response is a travel tip about sandwiches. The juxtaposition of a historic personal moment with completely trivializing morning-show advice is sharp cultural satire. The callback to the dumb-tips-drinking-game is paid off.

jokes.text: hey, baby, you new here? / yeah, this is my first show. / and before you worked here, were you an ass scientist? / because your ass blah, blah, blah. you get the point.
jokes.setup: Tracy hits on a new female crew member
jokes.punchline: He delivers a pick-up line about being an 'ass scientist' and then explicitly skips the rest: 'blah, blah, blah. you get the point.' — meta-abbreviated flirtation
jokes.explanation: A brilliant Tracy meta-joke. He starts a generic pickup line ('ass scientist') and then literally abbreviates it — 'blah blah blah, you get the point' — treating the completion as a waste of everyone's time. The self-aware skipping of the obvious conclusion is Tracy at his most genuinely clever. The joke is about the joke not needing to be finished. High marks for originality and economy.

jokes.text: so what's your name? / virginia. / virginia? but that's gonna be my daughter's name. / are you also someone's daughter? / uh, yeah. / is every woman someone's daughter? / of course. / uh oh!
jokes.setup: Tracy learns the new woman's name is Virginia — which is on his list of baby names
jokes.punchline: Tracy's philosophical interrogation of whether all women are someone's daughters, building to his own existential realization ('uh oh!') that he may have done something wrong with multiple women
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and Tracy philosophical spiral. The realization that his baby might be named Virginia and there's a Virginia standing in front of him triggers a Socratic examination of whether all women are daughters, culminating in 'uh oh!' which implies something very dark about Tracy's past. The callback to the baby name list and the escalating philosophical panic is perfectly structured.

jokes.text: her code — 5 5 2 8 7. / do you know what it means? / well, it's not a date. the first numbers are too high. / it's not the numbers, sir. it's the letters. they spell 'Klaus.' your name in german class.
jokes.setup: The voicemail code has been Nancy's secret; Kenneth realizes it spells KLAUS on a phone keypad
jokes.punchline: Nancy's password for years has been Jack's German class nickname — revealing she's been thinking about him the whole time
jokes.explanation: The episode's emotional anchor and structural payoff. The password reveal is both a comedic and emotional moment — it earns the comedy through the episodic setup (the entire break-in mission) and pays off the title's romantic subtext. Jack's deduction attempt ('it's not a date, the first numbers are too high') is a good character beat before Kenneth cracks it. Well-earned across the episode.

jokes.text: i'm just trying to figure out my next move. / you should buy a leather jacket! / get cerie in here. / not you.
jokes.setup: Jack says he needs to figure out how to pursue Nancy
jokes.punchline: Kenneth suggests a leather jacket; Jack immediately dismisses Kenneth and calls for Cerie — someone who actually understands cool
jokes.explanation: Quick efficient joke on Kenneth's social cluelessness and Jack's immediate course-correction. 'Not you' as the dismissal is perfectly calibrated — Kenneth is irrelevant to the cool-making process.

jokes.text: why did you even leave white haven, liz? / when was the last time you watched the sun rise? / sometimes at work — / or kissed a boy you just met? / gross. / or went dancing?
jokes.setup: Randy is challenging Liz to live more
jokes.punchline: Liz's responses — 'sometimes at work' for sunrise (sad), 'gross' for kissing a stranger — are perfect self-portraits of her hermit life
jokes.explanation: 'Sometimes at work' as an answer to 'when did you last watch a sunrise' implies Liz has pulled all-nighters at TGS, not sunrises by choice. 'Gross' for kissing strangers is vintage Liz. Good rapid-fire character beats.

jokes.text: i mean, who am i to tell jenna that she doesn't know how to be happy when i can't even figure out / stop so bored.
jokes.setup: Liz starts a philosophical speech about happiness
jokes.punchline: Cerie cuts her off mid-sentence with 'stop so bored' — the show's quickest shutdown of Liz's self-reflection
jokes.explanation: Excellent Cerie bit. 'Stop so bored' mid-sentence is maximum economy for maximum contempt. Cerie's dismissal of Liz's introspection without even hearing the point is perfectly characterizing both characters — Liz as someone whose self-reflection is tedious to others, Cerie as someone who processes emotions in five-word increments.

jokes.text: did i do that right? / yeah. / that was super bitchy. / you can't just break up with me. i'll sue you for breach of contract! / oh, you're being such a non pillow right now!
jokes.setup: Jenna and Franco are breaking up their fake relationship; Jenna breaks with emotion
jokes.punchline: Franco's frustrated outburst: 'You're being such a non pillow right now!' — the body pillow has become his baseline for acceptable human behavior
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'You're being such a non pillow right now' is extraordinary — it inverts the usual insult structure (comparing someone unfavorably to an inanimate object) and reveals that Franco's ideal partner IS an inanimate object. The logic is absurd but internally consistent. 'Non pillow' as a criticism of a person is both new vocabulary and a perfect character payoff. Highly quotable, excellent callback.

jokes.text: you can't just break up with me! I'll sue you for breach of contract! / Oh, you're being such a non-pillow right now!
jokes.setup: James Franco wants to break off the fake relationship.
jokes.punchline: 'You're being such a non-pillow right now!' — Franco's insult reveals that his frame of reference for ideal behavior is a body pillow.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Being such a non-pillow right now' is an insult that only makes sense in Franco's value system where a body pillow is the ideal companion. The implication that Jenna is failing to meet the standards set by an inanimate object is devastating and hilarious. The casual naturalism of using 'non-pillow' as an adjective is inspired. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: what am i doing, jenna? pretending to be something i'm not. making myself miserable when i've got happiness waiting for me at home. / unless kimiko's jealous of the ottoman. / there's nothing going on there. that's a business relationship.
jokes.setup: Franco has a breakthrough about returning to Kimiko
jokes.punchline: Jenna asks if Kimiko is jealous of the ottoman — introducing another inanimate object as a potential rival; Franco's 'that's a business relationship' is a perfect non-denial denial
jokes.explanation: Magnificent escalation of the Kimiko joke. The ottoman as a potential romantic rival implies an entire furniture-based emotional ecosystem in Franco's apartment. 'That's a business relationship' for the ottoman is a perfect corporate-speak deflection that simultaneously admits the ottoman is a relationship of some kind. The absurdity has its own internal logic now.

jokes.text: don't lemon your life, james. be happy.
jokes.setup: Jenna is urging Franco to pursue happiness with Kimiko
jokes.punchline: 'Don't lemon your life' — Jenna uses the earlier-coined verb meaning 'to royally screw something up,' applying it as life advice
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff on the 'lemoned' joke. The word has now made a full circuit: Jack coined it, Cerie validated it, and now Jenna uses it naturally. The meta-joke about Liz as a self-defeating archetype is fully established as vocabulary. 'Don't lemon your life' is both advice and a beautiful self-aware Liz joke.

jokes.text: i'm the actor james franco, damn it! and i'm in love with and common law married to a japanese body pillow!
jokes.setup: Franco's breakthrough moment of self-acceptance
jokes.punchline: He declares himself common law married to Kimiko — the full legal commitment is the comic escalation beyond mere love
jokes.explanation: The episode's Kimiko joke crescendo. The emotional release of 'I'm James Franco, damn it!' mirroring a traditional romantic declaration, but applied to a body pillow, is the full payoff of the Franco storyline. 'Common law married' is the perfect legal escalation — it implies they've been cohabitating long enough for the law to recognize the relationship. Highly quotable, excellent structure.

jokes.text: and i hope you had a good new year's. let me know the next time you and mark are in new york, and we'll all grab dinner.
jokes.setup: This is the end of Jack's voicemail — after the romantic German declaration, he pivots to a friendly sign-off to Nancy and her husband
jokes.punchline: Jack casually invites Nancy and her husband Mark to dinner — pivoting from romantic confession to social scheduling in the same message
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the voicemail. After a romantic German poetry recitation about long-suppressed feelings, Jack signs off with cheerful group dinner plans including the husband. The tonal whiplash is completely Jack — compartmentalizing a declaration of love into a polite social calendar item.

jokes.text: randy, this is james franco and our friend kimiko tan.
jokes.setup: Liz introduces Franco and Kimiko to Randy
jokes.punchline: Kimiko is introduced as a friend — a body pillow receiving a formal introduction to a human being
jokes.explanation: The visual joke of Liz formally introducing a body pillow as 'our friend Kimiko Tan' is a good final Kimiko beat. The social normalization — Liz playing along with the fiction — is a great small character moment and visual gag.

jokes.text: i blame you three for my unhealthy attitude towards women! you have created an atmosphere of hostility and intolerance that everyone talks about all the time.
jokes.setup: Tracy confronts Grizz, Dotcom, and Kenneth about something
jokes.punchline: His accusation — that they've created 'an atmosphere of hostility and intolerance that everyone talks about all the time' — implies everyone is gossiping about his entourage's attitude toward women
jokes.explanation: Tracy doing a big dramatic confrontation that's slightly undercooked — 'everyone talks about all the time' is a good overstatement but the setup needs more specificity to fully land. Functional but not the episode's best Tracy.

jokes.text: grizz, when was the last time you told your fiancee you loved her? / since the phone call i interrupted to make this announcement?
jokes.setup: Tracy demands to know when Grizz last told his fiancée he loved her
jokes.punchline: Grizz points out Tracy interrupted an actual phone call with his fiancée to stage this confrontation
jokes.explanation: Good comedic reversal — Tracy's feminist intervention is undermined by the fact that he literally interrupted Grizz telling his fiancée he loves her to ask when he last told his fiancée he loves her. The structure is tight and the irony lands cleanly.

jokes.text: kenneth, your haircut is disrespectful to lesbians!
jokes.setup: Tracy is going through his entourage's female-related failings
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's specific crime is that his haircut is 'disrespectful to lesbians' — an absurd category of offense that implies his haircut resembles a lesbian hairstyle in a mockable way
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist Tracy accusation. 'Disrespectful to lesbians' as a haircut critique is odd and specific in the right way — implying Kenneth has accidentally appropriated lesbian visual culture and done it badly. The category of grievance is new vocabulary for TV insults. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: dotcom, do you ever read books by women? / but george eliot was a woman.
jokes.setup: Tracy accuses Dotcom of not reading women authors
jokes.punchline: Dotcom's defense is George Eliot — correctly identifying that the Victorian novelist was a woman who published under a male pen name — which is a very Dotcom response (intellectual, correct, deflating Tracy's point)
jokes.explanation: A perfect Dotcom joke. His encyclopedic knowledge of literature deflects Tracy's broad feminist accusation with a precisely accurate historical fact — George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans) absolutely was a woman. The joke rewards educated viewers while also working as a character beat: Dotcom's intellect is always his comic tool. High character integration.

jokes.text: i've made a decision. and starting next week, i'm adding a woman to the entourage. / to be continued. / really?
jokes.setup: Tracy makes a big proclamation about adding a woman to his entourage
jokes.punchline: 'To be continued...' as a literal cliffhanger on Tracy's subplot, followed by Liz's 'Really?' — questioning whether this warrants a to-be-continued
jokes.explanation: A good meta-joke ending — 'to be continued' on a subplot of this absurdity, with Liz questioning the dramatic stakes, is a solid 30 Rock ending beat. The question of whether Tracy's entourage adding a woman warrants a cliffhanger is the joke.

tmdb_overview: Following a wild New Year's Eve, Jack has to try to repair the damage he did after leaving a drunken message on an ex's voicemail. Meanwhile, Jenna tries to get into a relationship with James Franco in order to cover up his secret; and Liz, after accidentally "outing" her cousin to his family, welcomes him to New York City; and Tracy finds new respect for women.
insight: Absurdist escalation reaches 90+ with 2.94 jokes-per-minute—30 Rock's densest sustained assault.
